## (c) What the MOEs allow us to say

Sampling error. The published 90 % MOE on a county's 1-year in-county share is 2.6 points for the median 1-year county (range 1.1-4.7; smallest in St. Louis, Greene, Jackson), so a single county's year-to-year change carries a 90 % half-width of 1.8-6.0 points and cannot, on its own, separate a 1-3 point step from noise; the per-county counts in (a) (9/21 in 2007, 2/21 in 2009) therefore understate what the survey says. What the MOEs do allow: (1) pooling the 16 Missouri counties cuts the MOE of the pooled share to about 0.54 points, and the pooled ACS change in 2006->07 (+0.31 +/- 0.75) and 2008->09 (-0.18 +/- 0.82) excludes the 2.1 and 1.4 point LODES drops in the same counties, so neither LODES step is present in the residence-based survey; (2) over 2010-2019 the pooled Missouri ACS slope is -0.02 +/- 0.06 pts/yr against a LODES slope of -0.25, and at the county level the ACS interval excludes a decline as steep as LODES in 10 of 21 counties (median sampling SE of a county slope 0.18 pts/yr, so only the larger counties and the steepest LODES declines are individually decisive). What they do not allow: a county-level verdict on steps of 1-3 points; any statement about counties under 65,000 before the 5-year series; and inference from the 5-year series as if its windows were independent (median 5-year share MOE 2.5 pts, but consecutive windows share 80 % of their sample, so adjacent 5-year changes are far more uncertain than the MOEs of two windows imply). MOEs also cover sampling error only, not the non-sampling differences in universe, place-of-work reporting and work-from-home treatment that produce the 15-20 point level gap between the two series.
